[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Maya Chen, Redwood, AE. Diego is our SE.
[00:06] Diego: hi all, Diego Alvarez here — I'll be walking through the integration bits. 
[00:12] Priya: Hey Maya, Priya here, joined by Tom and Jasmine. Good to see you.
[00:17] Tom: Yep, morning — afternoon — sorry, afternoon. Real quick, agenda: SDK handoff, show us an example with function calls returning structured JSON, and go over perf numbers from last week.
[00:27] Maya: Perfect. Diego do you want to start with the SDK story and the TypeScript example we promised?
[00:31] Diego: Sure. So we pushed a small sample repo — link in the notes — but the gist: the TS SDK supports streaming responses, function calls that return a JSON payload, and an option to validate output against a provided JSON schema on the client. The call looks like redwood.generate({model, input, functions}) or the streaming variant redwood.streamGenerate(...).
[00:50] Priya: Quick question — how deterministic is the function-calling flow? We need reliable structured output for our downstream parsers.
[00:56] Diego: Good question. With the current model family we recommend using the function-calling feature with a strict schema and post-call validation. The runtime will try to map to the function signature, but not 100% deterministic — so you should validate server-side and have a lightweight retry/fixup handler. Also prefix caching and prompt templates help.
[01:14] Jasmine: Are there existing helpers for retries? We don't want to write brittle glue code.
[01:18] Diego: Yes. The SDK includes a simple validator helper — it will attempt to coerce types for common mismatches (e.g., id as string vs number) and return a structured validation error object. It's basic but it avoids full custom parsers.
[01:31] Tom: Great. On perf we saw last week's numbers — 230ms median for 512 tokens with our internal stack. You mentioned Redwood had improvements when batching and KV cache are enabled?
[01:42] Maya: Right — in our hosted pilot we saw about 20–30% latency reduction when enabling continuous batching plus prefix (KV) caching on repetitive prompt prefixes. Note, in some of our transcripts KV cache got transcribed as KV cash earlier — small bug in the auto notes haha.
[01:56] Priya: Haha noted. Any gotchas for SDK instrumentation? We want token-level cost and latency breakdowns.
[02:02] Diego: The SDK emits request-level telemetry out of the box. For token-level breakdown you'll want to enable the optional tracing hook which streams per-chunk timings to the console/agent. We can forward that to your tracing backend (Jaeger/Datadog). We'll share config.
[02:16] Priya: That'd be helpful. Also curious about streaming partial outputs plus function-calling — e.g., emit partial structured chunks while model composes a long JSON — can we parse incrementally?
[02:28] Diego: Streaming can send partial tokens, but structured output mid-stream is tricky. We recommend generating the full JSON object and then stream only status/metadata while you wait. For very large payloads we have a chunked-output helper in the SDK to assemble pieces server-side.
[02:42] Tom: Understood. On the schema validation front — we tried our validator and still saw occasional fields missing. Is there a way to force the model to always include required fields?
[02:53] Diego: The best practice is: 1) use explicit instructions in the prompt template requiring 'always include fields X, Y, Z', 2) give the model an explicit function signature with types, and 3) run a post-generation fixer step. The runtime will prefer the function signature but sometimes the model will hallucinate or drop fields under truncation or token limits.
[03:10] Jasmine: Speaking of token limits — our front-end uses 4k context. Is there a cost hit if we bump to 8k? Any quantization strategies?
[03:19] Maya: Yes, longer context increases token cost linearly, but we have recommendations: use prefix caching for repeated templates, enable quantized model variants for lower memory/cost (we have int8 profiles), and route larger contexts to Dedicated pools if you need consistent latency.
[03:33] Priya: Any specific numbers for int8 vs fp16?
[03:36] Diego: We can run a quick bench — rough rule: int8 saves ~35–45% on GPU memory and cuts inference cost by ~20–30% depending on sequence length. We'll run exact for your workload.
[03:47] Tom: Cool. On error modes — if the function call fails (timeout or validation error), what's recommended fallback? We can't block the whole UI.
[03:56] Diego: Fallback patterns: return a lightweight degraded JSON (a summary with status: partial), trigger a synchronous small-model fallback for critical fields, or present the user with a TTL cached result. We'll show code patterns in the TS snippet.
[04:11] Priya: Excellent. Could you show the snippet now?
[04:14] Diego: Yep — I'm sharing the snippet in the chat: https://redwood.example/sdks/pilot-sample-repo — main points: 1) the generate call with functions array, 2) attach onValidationError hooks, 3) use streamGenerate for UI streaming.
[04:30] Tom: The sample looks good. One nit: our backend is Python-based — do you have the equivalent?
[04:35] Diego: There's a mirror in Python — same helpers. We'll include a Flask example calling the SDK and returning strict JSON to your service.
[04:42] Jasmine: For telemetry to our Datadog, do you support open-telemetry headers?
[04:47] Diego: Yes, we can propagate trace IDs and token-level spans. We'll add an example config to the repo.
[04:54] Maya: Quick reminder — for the pilot we'll run two perf variants: hosted + batching, and dedicated with int8. Diego will run the quantized comparison.
[05:02] Priya: Are there any security or compliance items blocking us? We need KMS integration and audit logs — also SOC2 scope.
[05:11] Maya: For Private/Dedicated we support customer KMS and audit logging; for hosted we have audit logs and RBAC. I'll attach our security pack (SOC2 summary, SSO/SAML guide, KMS options).
[05:23] Tom: Perfect. After that, we'll want a security deep dive with our infra/security folks.
[05:29] Maya: Let's block that next week. Tom, can you own scheduling?
[05:33] Tom: Yep, I'll coordinate.
[05:35] Priya: Quick clarifying question — how does the SDK surface model rollouts and pinning? We need to pin a specific model version for deterministic behavior in e2e tests.
[05:44] Diego: You can set modelVersion in the request and pin at the route level in the console. Rollouts can be canaryed with traffic percentages; we include the model_version and runtime build in logs for traceability.
[05:56] Jasmine: One more — when function-calling returns a list of objects, sometimes the model interleaves text commentary. Is there a way to force pure JSON?
[06:05] Diego: Use the function-only response mode — the runtime can request 'function_only' so the assistant won't emit extra prose. Also give explicit schema and use temperature=0 for more deterministic structure.
[06:18] Priya: Good to know.
[06:20] Maya: Okay let's move to open issues from last week — Priya you had a failing test around structured output?
[06:25] Priya: Yes — in our validation suite a single record had a null patient_id and it slipped through. I think it's a prompt template issue but we'll share the example.
[06:33] Diego: If you can dump the prompt and the full raw model output we'll triage; could be truncation or coercion. Often a minor schema mismatch causes silent coercion.
[06:42] Priya: I'll upload that to the pilot folder after the call.
[06:45] Tom: Also we noticed a spike in token usage when we tested long historical fetches — likely due to non-cached context. Any quick wins?
[06:55] Diego: Prefix caching + compacting the history (summarize older messages) helps a lot. We have an autosummarize preprocessor you can run to reduce tokens.
